facts.claim: Bob Dylan wrote "Masters of War" over the winter of 1962–63. It was released on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan in spring 1963.
The Freewheelin' version was recorded on April 24, 1963 and released by Columbia on May 27, 1963. John H. Hammond is credited as producer. (Songfacts gives the date as April 23.)
Freewheelin' was assembled from eight sessions at Columbia's Studio A, 799 Seventh Avenue, New York City, between April 1962 and April 1963.
Songfacts says Dylan did six takes of the song and the third is the one on the album.
The melody is taken from the traditional "Nottamun Town". Dylan borrowed the arrangement from folksinger Jean Ritchie's family version.

In the Freewheelin' liner notes Dylan said he had never written anything like it before. He said he doesn't sing songs hoping people will die, but couldn't help it with this one, calling it a reaction to the last straw.
In a September 10, 2001 interview Dylan said the song is not an anti-war song.
Late in the sessions Dylan told friends the album needed more "finger-pointin'" songs. "Masters of War" was the first result, an attack on the military-industrial complex.
Freewheelin' was Dylan's second album. He wrote 12 of its 13 songs after writing just two on his 1962 debut, and the album took his writing of contemporary words to traditional melodies further.
Dylan did not play an acoustic version of the song for 30 years after 1963, until a 1994 concert in Hiroshima, Japan. He performed it on stage 884 times between 1963 and 2016.

research.lineage: The song belongs to the early-1960s American folk revival and protest-song scene, and it sets new anti-war words to a traditional English-American folk melody.

draft:
The last thing the narrator of **Masters of War** promises is a graveside vigil. He'll follow the casket, watch it lowered, and stand there "'Til I'm sure that you're dead." It's one of the coldest closing lines in American song, and Bob Dylan knew it. In the Freewheelin' liner notes he said he'd never written anything like it, that he doesn't sing songs hoping people will die, but with this one he couldn't help it. He called it a reaction to the last straw.

That admission matters, because the fury here is only the surface. Read the song verse by verse and fear keeps showing through. The men who build the big guns and death planes never appear on the battlefield. They put the gun in someone else's hand and run when the bullets fly. The narrator is the one holding that gun, or expecting to. Then the song turns from the young dying in the mud to children who haven't been born yet: "Fear to bring children / Into the world." His own baby comes up next, unborn and unnamed. That's where the anger comes from: the threat to the life he hasn't started yet.

There's insecurity in it too. Halfway through, he answers the critics in his head, the ones who'd call him young and unlearned, and he settles the argument by saying even Jesus wouldn't forgive these men. He claims a moral certainty that he then uses to refuse forgiveness himself. The song never squares that, and it's stronger for leaving it alone. In a 2001 interview Dylan said it isn't an anti-war song. The lyric bears him out. It isn't pleading for peace. It's an accusation aimed at the people who profit from war.

The sound gives the anger no cover. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar holds a steady, unhurried pattern. The guitar rings clear and the room is small and dry. Dylan's voice is raspy, plain, and direct, with no harmonies and nothing added. The accompaniment never builds, so the escalation all happens in the words.

The tune is old. Dylan took the melody from the traditional "Nottamun Town," borrowing the arrangement from Jean Ritchie's family version. That was how Freewheelin' worked. On his second album he wrote 12 of the 13 songs and pushed further at setting new words to traditional melodies. Late in the sessions he told friends the record needed more "finger-pointin'" songs, and this was the first one he wrote. It was cut in spring 1963 at Columbia's Studio A with John H. Hammond producing, and Songfacts reports the album uses the third of six takes. Dylan wouldn't play it acoustic again for 30 years, until a 1994 concert in Hiroshima.

What stays with you is how calm the music is under all that rage, a voice keeping steady while it says something it can't take back.
